name: Erik Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a construction crew for the power company, so we build new lines rather than fix old ones. Right now it's a big housing estate going up on the old quarry land, and before that we spent four months running a line out to a solar farm. Setting poles, framing them, pulling wire, putting in transformers for streets that don't have houses yet. I like seeing a field turn into a lit-up street, and I don't like the mud, there's always mud.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ana, she's a receptionist at a dental practice. Saturdays I help my dad with his fencing business, he's had it twenty-five years, farm fences, gates, that kind of thing. We go to Mass most Sundays, more for my mother than anything, honestly. I've got about four months of savings, and I use the AI thing on my phone now and then, my cousin showed me, mostly for working out quotes for my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, it was a fancy calculator all along. Maybe a joke at the site about it. I wouldn't think about it much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me. Lots of building work, steady pay, Saturdays with my dad. That's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Keep saving, maybe put a bit toward a ring for Ana next year. Keep using the phone thing for my dad's quotes when it helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your work it already touches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The design side, the engineers use software to lay out where the poles go on a new estate. And the office uses it for scheduling. Out on site it's still us and the digger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your dad's business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Farmers still need fences. He'd be happy, he never liked computers anyway.

S0.say: I'd say it was a fancy calculator all along, maybe with a joke on site. I wouldn't think about it much more than that.
S0.think: It means nothing changes for me: plenty of building work, steady pay and Saturdays with my dad. That's fine by me.
S0.do: Keeps working on the construction crew and keeps saving, putting a bit toward an engagement ring for Ana next year. Uses the AI app for his father's fencing quotes when it helps.
S0.quote: There you go, it was a fancy calculator all along.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is settled and unfussy, with a second anchor in his father's fencing business. He already uses AI lightly for quotes. The plateau changes nothing he cares about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get on with it and adapt. Companies are going to use what's cheaper, that's just business. Nobody owes you the old way of doing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's actually good for my line of work. All these computers and data centres need power, so they're going to need more lines built, not fewer. I'd be busy for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, and once I saw what the other crews were using, I'd learn the new tools, maybe the robot pole setters or the drone surveys. I'd use the AI more for my dad's quotes and orders. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think it would mean more work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because last year we built two big lines just for a data centre outside town. That's AI, right there, eating power. More of that means more of us on the poles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything about Ana's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry for her, a bit. Reception's the sort of thing a computer could do, answering calls and booking. But she's good with people, and patients like her. I'd tell her to learn the new booking system before the others do.

S1.say: I'd say people need to get on with it and adapt, because companies will use what's cheaper. Nobody owes you the old way of doing things.
S1.think: Privately I think it's good for my line of work, because computers and data centres need power and more lines. I'd be busy for years.
S1.do: Keeps working and learns new tools such as robot pole setters or drone surveys once other crews are using them. Uses AI more for his father's quotes and orders.
S1.quote: That's AI, right there, eating power.
S1.fieldNote: Erik has a sharp, specific reason to feel safe: AI data centres need new lines, which means more construction work. His free-market view shows in accepting that companies will choose what's cheaper. His worry turns to Ana's reception job, not his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be hard, but families have to stick together and get through it. I wouldn't be asking the government to save me. I'd say that, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd hit me hard. If robots can set poles and pull wire, construction crews are the first to go, it's the easiest kind of line work to plan. I'd be out within a year, I reckon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time with my dad's fencing business straight away and help him get more customers. I'd cut back spending, push the savings to six months. And Ana and I would probably move in with my parents for a while to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd have something to do, that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to your dad's business. Wouldn't robots hit that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually, maybe. But farmers are slow to buy new things, and they like dealing with people they know. My dad's got twenty-five years of customers. That buys us some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the ring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait. I'd still want to marry her, but I'd want to have something steady first. She'd understand, she's practical.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be hard but families have to stick together and get through it. I wouldn't be asking the government to save me.
S2.think: Honestly it would hit me hard, because construction crews are the easiest line work to automate. I reckon I'd be out within a year.
S2.do: Goes full-time in his father's fencing business straight away and helps find more customers. Cuts spending, pushes savings to six months, postpones the engagement and moves in with his parents with Ana to save rent.
S2.feel: Anxious, but having something to do helps.
S2.quote: My dad's got twenty-five years of customers. That buys us some time.
S2.fieldNote: Erik's family business gives him a real fallback, which keeps him anxious rather than alarmed. He's frank that construction crews are the easiest line work to automate. He'd delay proposing until things were steady, and family comes before the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you're not lazy about it. People should learn a second trade or start something of their own. That's what I'd tell the guys on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means the line job ends, but I'd have time to build up my dad's business properly. Maybe get a robot post driver and do bigger jobs. Turn it into something I could take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my line job for a couple of years and work Saturdays with my dad, then go full-time once the business could pay me. I'd put some savings into a better machine for the fencing, maybe fifteen thousand. And I'd propose to Ana, probably next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. With two years it's a scramble. With five I can build the business up while I'm still getting a paycheque from the power company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your dad want that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble about the robot, but he'd want me to take over. He's been hinting about it for years. His back's not what it was.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you're not lazy, by learning a second trade or starting something. That's what I'd tell the guys on site.
S3.think: I think the line job ends, but I'd have time to build up my dad's business and maybe get a robot post driver for bigger jobs. I could turn it into something to take over.
S3.do: Keeps his line job for a couple of years while working Saturdays for his father, then goes full-time once the business can pay him. Invests about fifteen thousand from savings in a better fencing machine and proposes to Ana next year.
S3.quote: With two years it's a scramble.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Erik turn a fallback into a plan: build up the family business while still on the power company's payroll. He's willing to invest real savings in machinery. His father's bad back makes the handover feel natural.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty to prepare. Get a trade, start a business, look after your family. I'd say it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. Ten years is time to get married, have kids, and build up the fencing business with my dad. The line job would end, but I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the lines most of that time, it pays well. I'd save, get married, and buy a few machines for the fencing business over the years. I'd probably learn whatever AI stuff helps with running a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thirty-seven, ten years on. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running the business with my dad semi-retired, a couple of guys working for us, Ana and me with a kid or two. Maybe a robot or two for the heavy work. Sunday dinners at my mum's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd still be worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone has the same idea. If all the lineworkers start fencing businesses, there's not enough fences. And the big companies could come in with robots and undercut us.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare: get a trade, start a business and look after your family. I'd say it plainly.
S4.think: Privately I think I'd be all right, with time to marry, have children and build up the fencing business with my dad. The line job would end, but I'd see it coming.
S4.do: Keeps working the lines for most of the decade, saves, marries and gradually buys machines for the fencing business. Learns the AI tools that help run a small business.
S4.feel: A bit uneasy, but mostly fine.
S4.quote: If all the lineworkers start fencing businesses, there's not enough fences.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Erik pictures a full traditional life: the family business, children and Sunday dinners. His remaining worry is sharp and practical, too many people having the same fallback. He stays steady, moving step by step rather than all at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only one where I wouldn't have time to build anything. What would help is being able to keep the line job a bit longer while I build up the business, and maybe some help for small businesses to buy the new machines. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. Everyone talks about big companies and the government, but a lot of people like me have a dad or an uncle with a little business. That might be what saves a lot of us.

headlineQuote: A lot of people like me have a dad or an uncle with a little business. That might be what saves a lot of us.
portrait: Erik Costa is a 27-year-old construction lineworker building new lines for housing estates and solar farms, who spends Saturdays helping in his father's fencing business. He lives with his girlfriend Ana, a dental receptionist, has about four months of savings and uses AI now and then for quotes. He leans toward free markets and family self-reliance, and expects AI data centres to mean more line building in the milder pictures. Fast AGI makes him anxious but not lost, because the family business is a real fallback, and with more warning he plans to build it up and take it over.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it's the only picture where he wouldn't have time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping the line job a bit longer while he builds the business, and help for small businesses to buy new machines, as a fair start rather than handouts.
